It was a fine day for drying grain without the need to turn it. 
Fang Bai swept the courtyard with a broom, gently gathering the wheat ears scattered by the wind. The chicks followed closely behind, pecking at the flying chaff. 

A neighbor chatted idly over the fence, saying the wind had come and the weather would grow colder. After circling the topic a few times, she finally landed on the fact that he had no one to care for him. 
Without pausing his sweeping, Fang Bai grinned and gestured toward the flock of chicks: "I’ve got plenty of ‘family’ here, making noise all day and giving me headaches. If I added one more, I’d lose even this bit of peace. Ah, this talk is stifling—I need to go out to the fields for some fresh air." 
Before the words even faded, he was already striding out of the courtyard gate with a hoe on his shoulder, leaving the neighbor shaking her head with a sigh. 

The scattered grains in the field were well-hidden, hard for human eyes to spot, but the sparrows always knew where to find them. Fang Bai plowed slowly, keeping an eye on the flitting shadows. When a sparrow landed, he’d walk over and wave gently, startling the bird away before bending down to pick up the mud-stained grains. He’d blow off the dust and carefully tuck them into his pocket. 

The last two lantern persimmons at Yuxian Garden had just been bought by someone else—again. It had been like this for days. Fang Bai muttered that he was used to it. 
The sky shifted from deep blue to brilliant orange-red as he stood there, watching the sunset. Though he couldn’t get the lantern persimmons, at least he hadn’t missed the spectacle between heaven and earth. 
Lost in the sky, he didn’t notice where he was walking until a persimmon fell and hit his head. Overripe, it left his hair sticky. 
Holding the fruit in his palm, he wanted to tell someone—but when he looked up, there was only the persimmon tree. 

Loneliness lingered like a ghost. He thought of adding an ending to the supernatural tale he’d written for himself. The story was about a golden-furred spirit beast, reborn as a dog with the lowly name Huang, yet still believing itself to be a lion. Though trapped in a domestic yard, it behaved oddly—chasing neither cats nor rabbits, eating no scraps, shirking its duties as a dog—until it was finally struck dead by lightning. 
Back at the stone table in his courtyard, the ink stains were mixed with chaff left by the chicks. Picking up a grain, Fang Bai felt a sudden inspiration and took up his brush again. In the moment before Huang’s spirit faded, a flock of birds carried dew in their beaks, sheltering its body with their wings as if performing a funeral rite. Then its golden form dissolved, its light smoke merging with the dawn mist. 
This peaceful, warm end, surrounded by poultry… didn’t seem so bad after all. 

In the distance, a group of young men were shouting something. As he drew closer, he saw their disheveled clothes, their hands clutching maps, their faces blank with confusion. Their white robes were stained with mud and dust. 
Fang Bai was about to tease them when he met the dazed eyes of the five. The moment they spotted him, their faces lit up in unison. They stumbled over each other, tripping and scrambling until they finally reached him, only to collapse in a heap. 
"Uncle Fang! Uncle Fang! You’re Uncle Fang, right?" 
Fang Bai recognized their robes immediately but feigned disdain. "My dear senior brother’s disciples are getting dumber by the batch, huh?" 
The young men burst into tears. Their weeping was unsettling. The orange-red sky was now stained by a sunset the color of blood. 
"Uncle… our Inkbound Order… it’s gone…" 

The wind had indeed come. And the sky—it would grow colder.
